description_full: Getty Realty Corp. is a publicly traded, net lease REIT specializing in the acquisition, financing and development of convenience, automotive and other single-tenant retail real estate. As of June 30, 2026, the Company's portfolio included 1,224 freestanding properties located in 46 states across the United States and Washington, D.C. Getty Realty Corp. was incorporated in 1955 and is based in New York, United States.

financial_summary: Getty Realty Corporation is a small-cap real estate business with a $1.9B market cap on $222M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +3.0pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $127M in free cash flow — roughly 57 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.61× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 5.6% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 57% operating margin runs 34pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.87x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 12% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 21% and a beta of 0.45, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.24 vs 5y 0.38), so read it loosely.
About $15.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 47% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 49% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 32% below its DCF fair value of $41.84, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 45%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $29.38 to $62.05 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/E 17.4 vs 23.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 17% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $33.86 on average, 19% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It converts 57% of revenue into free cash flow, or 54% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.61x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 57%.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.1% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.2x net debt to EBITDA ($8.4M of cash against $995.0M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.7x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.34 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.2% over 3 years, 8.5% over 5 years and 7.2% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.0% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 9.0% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (0.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 5.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 89%.
It returns 5.7% a year to shareholders (7.0% in dividends).
The share count has grown 7.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 118% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 31 employees, each generates about $7.2M of revenue, 3.1x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 4.9% a year.
That works out to $4.1M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.3M (0x revenue per employee).
